name: unknown-jank-just-under-threshold
capturedFrom: probe/riverpod_probe on device A015 (Android 16, Flutter 3.44.1), 2026-08-26. 45-second window covering all five workload phases (tick, invalidate, throw, navigate, idle).
why:
'Unknown' is the correct answer for diagnose_runtime here, and this is the most valuable kind of incident to pin: the one where a confident answer would be wrong.

There is no runtime fault. Zero exceptions — the probe's throw phase raises inside a provider, which Riverpod captures as an AsyncError, so nothing reaches FlutterError.onError and no exception is observable. Zero network events. All 41 log lines are severity info. No memory growth signal.

What the session does have is 74 of 381 frames janky (19.4%) — real, but below the 20% the jank hypothesis requires, and deliberately so: a fifth of frames missing budget on a device under a synthetic storm is not evidence that something is broken. With no hypothesis firing, abstaining is the honest response, and the summary tells the reader to reproduce the problem while connected.

Note that this is not the tool being blind. diagnose_performance answers the same session confidently and correctly (0.9): build-bound, mean build 26.51ms against 1.98ms raster. The division is the point — the runtime question is 'what is wrong', and the answer is 'nothing I can name'.

The near miss is what makes this a sharp guard. 19.4% against a 20% threshold means any careless loosening turns this into a confident jank verdict on a session with no fault at all, and false confidence is the failure this project cares about most.

collectors.name: state
collectors.detail: Observing riverpod activity. Counted only: each event carries an opaque pointer, not a provider name or value, and no service extension exists to resolve it. A provider event means dependents were notified, so the count is not a count of state changes.

runtime.summary: Unknown — insufficient runtime evidence. Runtime activity captured but no exceptions, jank pattern, or network errors were found.
limitations: No network evidence in this session. HTTP capture is pull-on-demand and Dart-side only — platform-code and WebView traffic is never visible.
No memory samples captured. Call get_memory, or open the dashboard, to include memory in future diagnoses.
VM timeline events are fetched on demand and not stored, so they take no part in correlation.
Only Dart-side runtime state is observed. A cause in platform (Kotlin/Swift) code or in a WebView cannot appear here.

confidenceBreakdown.basis: Conservative heuristic scored from corroborating evidence, not a calibrated probability. Below 0.7 the status is "unknown" rather than a guess.

recommendedFixes: The app appears healthy. Reproduce the issue while connected, then diagnose again.

performance.summary: 74/381 frames (19%) exceeded the 16.67ms budget. Worst 55.49ms, p99 50.17ms. Dominated by the build phase.

findings.claim: 9058 widget rebuild(s) across 76 frame(s). Busiest: DetailScreen at riverpod_probe/lib/main.dart:60 — 3 rebuild(s) over 3 frame(s).
findings.fix: Narrow the rebuild scope around DetailScreen at riverpod_probe/lib/main.dart:60. Split the widget so only the part that depends on changing state rebuilds, add const constructors, and move computation out of build().

findings.claim: Janky frames spend most of their time building: mean build 26.51ms vs raster 1.98ms.
findings.fix: Build-phase heavy: move expensive work out of build(), use const widgets, cache computed values, and narrow the rebuild scope with smaller widgets or selectors.

findings.claim: 51 of 74 janky frames (69%) fell within 1000ms of riverpod state activity (50 events). For comparison, 34% of the 307 smooth frames were also inside a window.
findings.fix: Correlation only, and the window is symmetric, so this does not show the state change came first. Provider names are not observable from here either: call get_rebuilds to see which widgets rebuilt in these frames, then narrow what those widgets watch (select/family providers) so one change stops rebuilding the whole subtree.

limitations: No CPU sampling. A slow build can be attributed to a widget, but not to a specific function — use the DevTools CPU profiler for that.
GC events are not observable: the VM timeline is fetched on demand and not stored, so garbage-collection pauses cannot be ruled in or out.
Frames are only captured while connected, and older ones roll out of the retention window.
State changes are counted, never read: neither Riverpod nor Provider exposes values or provider names through the VM Service, so no claim is made about which provider is responsible.
Rebuild totals cover the busiest locations in each frame, not every rebuild — the long tail is counted but not itemised.
App-versus-package attribution is a path heuristic: getPubRootDirectories is empty until a DevTools client sets it, so there is no authoritative project root.

notes: 3 frame(s) rebuilt more locations than are retained; totals cover the busiest locations per frame, not every rebuild.
